summary: In Greek mythology, Bias (Ancient Greek Βίας) is a Trojan — counted by Apollodorus among Priam's sons by other women — and the father of the warriors Laogonus and Dardanus, whom Achilles thrusts from their chariot in Iliad 20. Distinct from Bias son of Amythaon, from Homeric Bias of Pylos and Athens, and from the Dulichian suitor of Penelope.
etymology: Ancient Greek Βίας (Bias); Latin Biantes. Several unrelated heroes share the name; this node is fixed by the Laogonus–Dardanus patronymic and the Trojan theatre.

sections.heading: Father of Laogonus and Dardanus
paragraphs: In Iliad 20 Achilles, raging after other Trojans, sets upon Laogonus and Dardanus, sons of Bias, and thrusts both from their chariot — one with a cast of the spear, the other with the sword in close fight. Apollodorus lists Bias among Priam's many sons by women other than Hecuba, in the long roll beside Dryops, Lycaon, and Chromius.
A minority notice has Bias himself slain by Idomeneus together with brothers Dryops and Chorithan; the atlas keeps bias-trojan as the Iliadic father of the chariot-pair Achilles kills.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: Not bias-aeolid (Amythaon's Argive king, brother of Melampus); not bias-pylian (Nestor's "shepherd of the host"); not bias-athenian (Menestheus' companion at the ships); not bias-dulichium (Penelope's suitor). Wikipedia gathers these and a Megarian prince Bias son of Lelex on one disambiguation page.
